title: Complaining and protesting
subtitle: this is just not on, take exception to, whinge
summary: Complain at exactly the right level of formality, from 'Look here!' to 'I take great exception to ...', and choose between grumble, gripe, grouse and whinge.

lesson.heading: Informal complaints
lesson.text: These are for friends, family and people you know well. Within the group they run roughly from weaker to stronger, though much depends on who you are speaking to. **This is just not on** means simply unacceptable, and **Enough is enough!** says you will put up with no more.

examples.text: **You've got to do something about** that window of yours. It rattles in the wind and keeps me awake.
**For goodness' sake!** I'm **fed up with** / **sick of** all your moaning and grumbling. Cheer up!
**Look here!** I've just about **had enough of** your stupid comments.
Look, **this is just not on!** You promised to be here by two o'clock and it's almost three!
**Enough is enough!** Please, no more arguments - be nice to each other!

lesson.heading: Neutral complaints
lesson.text: These work in almost any situation. Notice **I wish you would** + verb for something you want someone to start doing, and **I wish you wouldn't** + verb for something you want them to stop. **It just won't do!** means the situation cannot be allowed to continue.

examples.text: I'm **not at all satisfied with** the service I've received.
**Something will have to be done about** that pile of rubbish. It can't be left in front of the house.
**I wish you would** turn your radio down.
**I wish you wouldn't** play your music so loudly.
You never help around the house. **It just won't do!** You're going to have to change your ways.

lesson.heading: Formal complaints
lesson.text: These belong in letters, emails and dealings with organisations, typically about bad service or behaviour. **I wish to complain about ...** opens a formal letter; **most unsatisfactory**, **unacceptable** and **shameful** grade the offence upwards. **Shameful** means it should make you feel embarrassed and guilty.

examples.text: **I wish to complain about** the delay in delivering my order.
The carpet in my room is stained and dirty. **This is most unsatisfactory.**
**I take great exception to** your unfair comments about our committee.
**I really must object to** being made to wait so long before seeing the manager.
The water pipe you have repaired three times is leaking again. **This is simply unacceptable.**
Your bus driver left the children by the roadside in pouring rain with no adult in attendance. **This is shameful.**

lesson.heading: Verbs and nouns for complaining
rows: strongly express complaint, disapproval or disagreement
complain to someone, or about something; formal
criticise or complain about even small mistakes
complain in a quiet but angry way

lesson.text: **Object to** is followed by a noun, a pronoun or an **-ing** form: I object to **being made** to wait - never ~~object to be made~~.

lesson.heading: Complaining indirectly
lesson.text: Much English complaint is deliberately understated, especially in reports, references and appraisals. The polite surface hides a firm criticism, and advanced learners need to hear what is really being said.

examples.text: 'It doesn't smell very nice in here!'
examples.note: Open the window - the room needs cleaning.

examples.text: 'Jorge tends to complete his work rather too quickly.'
'Punctuality is not Simone's highest priority.'
'You'd be well advised to reassess your long-term plans.'
examples.note: You are not suited to this job.

examples.text: 'It would benefit from a lick of paint.'

lesson.heading: Saying the same thing at two levels

left.label: Informal
examples: **Look here!** I've just about had enough of your rudeness!
You've **got to do something about** the state of your desk.
The delay with my order is **just not on**.

right.label: Formal
examples: I **take great exception to** your rudeness.
The state of your desk **is most unsatisfactory**.
The delay in completing my order is **simply unacceptable**.

exercises.explanation: Whinge, grumble, gripe, grouse and complain all take about.

exercises.prompt: We ___ great exception to the proposed plans.
exercises.explanation: To take great exception to something is a formal way of objecting strongly.

exercises.prompt: They objected loudly to ___ forced to sit on the floor because there were no chairs.
exercises.explanation: Object to is followed by a noun, pronoun or -ing form - never the base form of the verb.

exercises.prompt: He's always writing letters to the newspaper, finding fault ___ something or other.
exercises.explanation: To find fault with something is to criticise even its smallest mistakes.

exercises.prompt: Something will have to be ___ about traffic problems in the city.
exercises.explanation: Something will have to be done about ... is a neutral, all-purpose complaint.

exercises.prompt: I wish people ___ talk loudly on their phones when I'm on the train.
exercises.explanation: I wish you wouldn't + verb asks someone to stop doing something.

exercises.prompt: This standard of work just won't ___!
exercises.explanation: It just won't do! means the situation cannot be allowed to continue.

exercises.prompt: I heard her remonstrating ___ a police officer about the road being closed.
exercises.explanation: You remonstrate with somebody, but remonstrate about something.

exercises.prompt: I'm tired of hearing you constantly moaning. Enough is ___!
exercises.explanation: Enough is enough! says that you will put up with no more.

exercises.prompt: Would you expect each complaint in an informal or a formal situation?

items.text: Look here! I've just about had enough of your rudeness!
You've got to do something about the state of your desk.
I am writing to remonstrate about some injustices in your regulations.
I wish to complain about the poor facilities at the station.
The delay in completing my order is simply unacceptable.

exercises.prompt: Match each indirect complaint with what the speaker really means.

pairs.left: Jorge tends to complete his work rather too quickly.
Punctuality is not Simone's highest priority.
pairs.right: Simone is often late for work.

pairs.left: You'd be well advised to reassess your long-term plans.
pairs.right: You are not suited to this job.

pairs.left: It would benefit from a lick of paint.
The TV seems to be a bit loud.

exercises.prompt: Which verb means to complain in a quiet but angry way?
exercises.explanation: To grumble is to complain quietly but angrily; protest is to complain strongly and openly.

options: I object to being made to wait an hour.
I object to be made to wait an hour.
I object being made to wait an hour.
I object for being made to wait an hour.
exercises.explanation: Object to takes a noun, a pronoun or an -ing form.

exercises.prompt: You are writing a formal email to a newspaper about factory noise at night. Which opening is right?
options: Most people take considerable exception to being awoken by loud noise from the factory.
Look here! I've had just about enough of that factory!
For goodness' sake, this is just not on!
I'm fed up with all this racket.
exercises.explanation: Take exception to belongs to formal written complaints; the others are informal.

exercises.prompt: You are complaining to a close friend about having to work longer hours. Which is most natural?
options: I've just about had enough of working longer hours.
I wish to complain about the revised working hours.
I take great exception to the revised working hours.
exercises.explanation: I've just about had enough of ... is the informal register you use with a close friend.

exercises.statement: If behaviour is described as shameful, it is meant to make the people responsible feel embarrassed and guilty.
exercises.explanation: Correct - shameful is one of the strongest formal words of complaint.

exercises.statement: Whinge, gripe and grouse are all formal words for complaining.
exercises.explanation: No - all three are informal. The formal verb is remonstrate.

exercises.prompt: Put this formal complaint in order.
exercises.answer: I really must object to being made to wait so long
exercises.explanation: Object to is followed by an -ing form, here the passive being made.
